Clinical Reference · Nephrology

SIADH — Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuresis

On this page
SIADH is euvolemic, hypotonic hyponatremia from inappropriate ADH (vasopressin) action — the kidney retains free water it should be dumping, so serum sodium falls while the urine stays inappropriately concentrated.
Euvolemic · Uosm >100 · UNa >30 Serum osm <275 mOsm/kg Correct ≤8 mmol/L/24h if ODS-risk First line: fluid restriction + treat cause Most common inpatient dysnatremia
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

SIADH is a disorder of water excess, not salt deficiency. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH / arginine-vasopressin, AVP) is released when it shouldn't be — not in response to a high osmolality or low volume, but "inappropriately" (from a lung tumor, an inflamed brain or lung, a drug, pain, or nausea). AVP binds V2 receptors on the collecting-duct principal cells → cAMP → aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels are trafficked into the apical membrane → the duct becomes water-permeable → free water is reabsorbed back into the body while the urine stays inappropriately concentrated (Uosm >100).

That retained water dilutes the plasma → hyponatremia with a low serum osmolality (<275 mOsm/kg). The modest water-driven volume expansion then suppresses aldosterone and raises natriuretic peptides, so the kidney spills sodium into the urine (UNa >30–40). The result is the SIADH fingerprint: a clinically euvolemic patient with low serum osmolality, high urine osmolality, and high urine sodium. The natriuresis is volume-mediated — it is not a primary salt leak, which is why "just give salt" does not fix it.

the body is a swimming pool with the fill-valve stuck "on" (AVP). Water trickles in and the pool's salt concentration drops (hyponatremia). A float switch notices the pool is a little too full and opens a drain that lets out salty water (natriuresis) — but the fill-valve is still open, so the pool stays diluted. To fix the salt level you must turn off the valve (fluid restriction / vaptan) or add solute so each litre of urine carries more water out — not scoop salt into a pool that keeps refilling.
The SIADH cascade: inappropriate ADH → V2/aquaporin-2 water retention → dilutional hyponatremia + volume-mediated natriuresis → euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia → cerebral edema.
ADH binds the V2 receptor on the collecting-duct principal cell, driving aquaporin-2 water channels to the apical membrane so water is reabsorbed — the exact step SIADH turns on inappropriately.
Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. Source
Where it happens along the nephron. Loop diuretics wash out the medullary gradient (thick ascending limb) so the collecting duct can't concentrate — one lever we pull in SIADH.
Nephron secretion & reabsorption — OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0. Source
every SIADH therapy attacks one step of the cascade. Fluid restriction starves the water input. Salt tablets / oral urea / high-protein diet raise daily solute excretion — because AVP fixes Uosm high, more solute obligates more urine water loss (osmotic diuresis). Loop diuretics wash out the medullary gradient so the duct can't concentrate even with AVP present. Vaptans (tolvaptan) competitively block the V2 receptor → AQP2 is withdrawn → electrolyte-free "aquaresis." Hypertonic 3% saline adds sodium faster than the kidney can excrete it — the only rapid fix for symptomatic cerebral edema. Demeclocycline induces a nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (renal AVP resistance).
📖

Diagnostic criteria, severity & subtypes

Bartter–Schwartz criteria (1967 — still the standard)

Essential (all required): effective serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg; serum Na <135 mmol/L; urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg; urine Na >30 mmol/L (European threshold; classically >20) on normal salt/water intake; clinical euvolemia; normal thyroid & adrenal function with no recent diuretics. Supportive: serum uric acid <4 mg/dL, low BUN, fractional excretion of urate >12%, fractional excretion of urea >55%, failure to correct with 0.9% saline, correction with fluid restriction.

Severity — biochemical vs symptomatic (2014 European guideline)

By sodium levelRangeBy symptomsFindings
Mild130–135 mmol/LModerately severeNausea (no vomiting), confusion, headache
Moderate125–129 mmol/LSevereVomiting, cardiorespiratory distress, deep somnolence, seizures, coma (GCS ≤8)
Profound<125 mmol/L—Symptom severity — not the number alone — drives how aggressively you treat
Acute (<48 h) vs chronic (≥48 h or unknown) is the single most important split for treatment. Brain volume adaptation (extrusion of organic osmolytes) takes ~24–48 h. In acute hyponatremia the unadapted brain swells → cerebral-edema risk dominates → you can correct more aggressively. In chronic hyponatremia the adapted brain is vulnerable to osmotic demyelination if re-corrected too fast → strict rate limits apply. If duration is unknown, treat as chronic.

SIAD subtypes (Robertson AVP-response pattern)

Type~SharePatternClassic example
A~30–40%Erratic, unregulated AVP releaseSmall-cell lung cancer (ectopic AVP)
B~30%Constant low-level AVP "leak"Chronic pulmonary/CNS disease
C~15%Reset osmostat — normal regulation around a lower set-point; dilutes/concentrates normallyChronic illness, pregnancy — usually needs no treatment
D~10%AVP undetectable yet inappropriate antidiuresis — nephrogenic SIAD (gain-of-function V2 mutation)Hereditary NSIAD — does not respond to vaptans

CategoryExamples
CNSStroke, hemorrhage, meningitis/encephalitis, trauma, tumor, Guillain–Barré, hydrocephalus
PulmonaryPneumonia (bacterial/viral), TB, empyema, asthma, positive-pressure ventilation
Malignancy (ectopic AVP)Small-cell lung cancer (classic), head & neck, olfactory neuroblastoma
DrugsSSRIs/SNRIs (elderly), carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, cyclophosphamide (IV high-dose), vincristine, antipsychotics, TCAs, MDMA/"ecstasy," NSAIDs, desmopressin/oxytocin, chlorpropamide
OtherPain, nausea, postoperative state, HIV, hereditary NSIAD

Chest radiograph of an apical (Pancoast) lung tumour. A central hilar or apical mass on CXR is the SIADH screen in a smoker.

⚠️

Two traps: mimics & the demyelination danger

Cerebral salt wasting (CSW) vs SIADH — volume status is the key

Both give hyponatremia with high urine Na and high Uosm, usually after an intracranial insult. The difference: CSW = true hypovolemia (primary renal salt wasting → volume depletion → secondary appropriate ADH), whereas SIADH = euvolemia. CSW improves with salt + volume repletion; SIADH worsens with volume and needs fluid restriction. Misclassifying CSW as SIADH and restricting fluids can be dangerous. Many experts consider CSW rare/over-diagnosed.

FeatureSIADHCSW
Volume statusEuvolemicHypovolemic (orthostasis, dry)
Primary problemWater retentionRenal sodium wasting
ADHInappropriate (primary)Appropriate (secondary to low volume)
TreatmentFluid restrictionSalt + volume repletion
Response to saline challengeNa drops / no improvementNa improves

Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS / central pontine myelinolysis)

Correcting chronic hyponatremia too fast strips water from adapted brain cells faster than they can re-accumulate osmolytes → demyelination of the pons (and extrapontine sites). It is classically biphasic: initial improvement, then days later dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis, "locked-in" syndrome. Prevention is everything — there is no reliable treatment once established.

Central pontine myelinolysis on brain MRI — the feared consequence of over-rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia.
CPM MRI — Dr Frank Gaillard, Radiopaedia/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0. Source
ODS risk factors (2013 US Expert Panel) mandate the strictest correction limits: serum Na ≤105 mmol/L, hypokalemia, alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, advanced liver disease. In any of these, cap the 24-h rise at ≤8 mmol/L (aim 4–6) and consider a proactive DDAVP clamp.

Assess

When to suspect & how it presents

🔍

Presentation — symptom, frequency & why it happens

Most chronic SIADH is found incidentally on a metabolic panel. Symptoms track both the absolute sodium and, more importantly, the rate of fall — a slow drop to 120 may be nearly silent, while a fast drop to 128 can seize. Suspect it in an elderly patient on an SSRI, a smoker, or anyone with pneumonia, a CNS event, or unexplained euvolemic hyponatremia.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens
Nausea / malaise~30–50%Early marker of osmotic brain-cell swelling; an early "moderately-severe" symptom
Gait instability / falls2–4× riskSubtle cerebral dysfunction even with "mild" chronic hyponatremia → attention & balance impaired
Headache~20–40%Raised intracranial pressure from osmotic water shift into brain
Cognitive slowing / confusion~20–40%Neuronal swelling; worsens with lower Na and faster fall
Muscle cramps / weakness~15–30%Altered membrane excitability from hypotonicity
Seizures<10%Severe/acute cerebral edema (usually Na <120 and/or acute) — a medical emergency
Obtundation / coma / respiratory arrest<5%Brainstem compression from severe cerebral edema; non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema can accompany
In the elderly, "mild" chronic hyponatremia is not benign — it independently raises the risk of falls, fractures, and osteoporosis. Don't shrug at a sodium of 130.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

The diagnostic sequence (2014 European algorithm)

SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion — work osmolality → volume → urine, then rule out the mimics.

Serum osmolalityFirst step. Must be <275 mOsm/kg to confirm true hypotonic hyponatremia. Excludes pseudohyponatremia (hyperlipidemia/paraprotein) and translocational (hyperglycemia, mannitol).Step 1
Urine osmolality≤100 → primary polydipsia / low solute (beer potomania). >100 with euvolemia → points to SIADH.Step 2
Urine sodium>30 mmol/L (off diuretics) supports SIADH; <30 suggests low effective circulating volume (GI/renal loss, HF, cirrhosis).Step 3
Clinical volume examEuvolemia is required. Look for orthostasis/dryness (hypovolemia) or edema/JVD (hypervolemia) to exclude mimics.Step 4
TSH + AM cortisolMandatory before labeling SIADH. Hypothyroidism and — critically — glucocorticoid (adrenal) deficiency mimic SIADH and can be fatal if missed. Short Synacthen if borderline.Step 5
Uric acid + BUNLow uric acid (<4 mg/dL) and low BUN support SIADH (dilution + increased urate clearance). Normal/high uric acid argues for volume depletion instead.Supportive
Med reviewSSRIs/SNRIs, carbamazepine, thiazides, antipsychotics — often the whole cause. Stopping the drug may be the treatment.Always
CXR ± CT chest / CNS imagingScreen for small-cell lung cancer (smoker, unexplained SIADH) and CNS causes when clinically suggested.If indicated

How to read each lab — and what fools you

LabSIADH directionMechanism & confounders
Serum osmolalityLow (<275)Dilution by retained water. False-normal/high with hyperglycemia, mannitol, alcohol, or paraprotein (measured osm gap).
Urine osmolalityHigh (>100)Persistent AVP prevents maximal dilution. Falsely low if patient just water-loaded before the sample.
Urine sodiumHigh (>30–40)Volume-mediated natriuresis. Falsely low on a low-salt diet, recent vomiting, or overlapping hypovolemia.
Serum uric acidLow (<4)Dilution + increased fractional urate excretion. Rises after correction — a useful confirmatory trend.
Serum Na (measured)LowTrue dilution. Correct for glucose: add ~2.4 mmol/L per 100 mg/dL glucose above normal before interpreting.
Calculate

Will fluid restriction work? (Furst ratio)

The Furst ratio = (urine Na + urine K) ÷ serum Na predicts whether fluid restriction alone can raise the sodium. Enter values (mmol/L):

—
Enter values to see the recommended restriction.

Thresholds (2014 European guideline): >1 → restriction unlikely to work (consider urea/vaptan); 0.5–1 → restrict to <500 mL/day; <0.5 → restrict to <1 L/day.

Treat

Chronic management ladder

💊

First-line → escalation (with full dose ladders)

Always treat the cause first: stop the offending drug (SSRI, carbamazepine, thiazide), treat pneumonia, address malignancy. For many outpatients that alone corrects the sodium.
1
Fluid restriction (first-line, chronic)
Target <800–1000 mL/day total fluids
▾
drives free-water balance negative by putting intake below urine + insensible losses. Fails when urine is very concentrated — check the Furst ratio above.
  • Start: <1000 mL/day of all fluids (not just water). Titrate down to 500–750 mL/day if Furst 0.5–1 or if no response.
  • Target: Na rise of 4–8 mmol/L over several days; recheck Na in 2–3 days, then weekly.
  • Counsel: count soups, ice, coffee; a high dietary salt/protein intake helps (raises solute).
2
Increase solute — oral urea / salt / protein
When restriction alone is inadequate or impractical
▾
because AVP fixes urine osmolality high, every extra osmole of solute obligates more urine water loss (osmotic diuresis) → net free-water excretion.
AgentStartTitrate → Target/MaxWhy it worksIf intolerant / alt
Oral urea15 g/day (0.25 g/kg) in juice↑ to 0.25–0.5 g/kg/day; max ~30–45 g/dayOsmotic diuretic; endorsed by 2014 European guideline; no ODS signalBitter — mix with citrus/sweetener; if refused → salt+loop
NaCl (salt) tablets1 g with meals1–3 g TID (add ~3–9 g/day)Adds excreted solute; best combined with a loop diureticDietary salt/high-protein diet; watch BP/edema
High-protein dietDietaryAs toleratedGenerates urea → endogenous osmotic soluteProtein supplement drinks
3
Loop diuretic + salt
Furosemide to impair urine concentrating ability
▾
loop diuretics block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb → wash out the medullary gradient → the collecting duct cannot concentrate urine even with AVP present → more free water excreted.
AgentStartTitrate → MaxWhy it worksIf allergic / alt
Furosemide20 mg PO daily20 → 40 mg daily (BID if needed)Abolishes medullary gradient; pair with oral NaCl to avoid volume depletionSulfa allergy → ethacrynic acid 25–50 mg (non-sulfonamide loop)
Torsemide (alt)10 mg PO daily10 → 20 mg dailyLonger-acting loop; same mechanism, more predictable oral absorptionEthacrynic acid if true sulfa allergy
Monitor K and renal function; loop + salt is a classic, cheap, effective combination for chronic SIADH before reaching for vaptans.
4
Vasopressin antagonist (tolvaptan) — specialist
Refractory; hospital-initiated only
▾
tolvaptan competitively blocks the V2 receptor → aquaporin-2 withdrawn → pure electrolyte-free water diuresis ("aquaresis") with little sodium loss (SALT-1/-2, NEJM 2006).
AgentStartTitrate → MaxWhy it worksCautions / alt
Tolvaptan15 mg PO once daily15 → 30 → up to 60 mg/dayV2 antagonist aquareticHospital initiation, free water access (no fluid restriction during start-up), Na monitoring; ≤30 days; avoid in liver disease (FDA hepatotoxicity boxed warning); never co-give with 3% saline
Demeclocycline (historical)300 mg PO BID300 → 600 mg BID (600–1200 mg/day)Induces nephrogenic DI (renal AVP resistance)Slow (3–4 d), nephrotoxic, photosensitizing; 2014 European guideline suggests against it and against lithium
Tolvaptan can raise Na too fast — this is exactly why it is started in hospital with frequent Na checks, no concurrent fluid restriction, and no 3% saline. Keep the 24-h rise <8 mmol/L.
Allergy / intolerance quick-mapSalt tablets not tolerated → urea. Tolvaptan contraindicated (liver disease) or unaffordable → urea ± furosemide + salt. Sulfa allergy limiting furosemide → ethacrynic acid, or rely on urea + fluid restriction.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidities change the course & the plan

ComorbidityEffect on SIADHManagement change
Advanced liver disease / cirrhosisBaseline hyponatremia; high ODS risk; hypervolemic mimicAvoid tolvaptan (hepatotoxicity); cap correction ≤8 mmol/L/24h; DDAVP clamp
Heart failureHypervolemic hyponatremia mimic — not true SIADHTreat with diuresis + guideline HF therapy, not fluid restriction alone; check volume
Alcohol use disorder / malnutritionMajor ODS risk factors; low solute intake (beer potomania mimic)Strictest correction limits; replete K, phosphate, thiamine; count K toward Na budget
Depression on SSRI/SNRICommon drug cause, especially elderlyStop/switch the antidepressant; may resolve SIADH entirely
Epilepsy on carbamazepine/oxcarbazepineClassic drug causeSwitch antiepileptic in conjunction with neurology
Small-cell lung cancerEctopic AVP; SIADH may be paraneoplastic markerTreating the tumor (chemo) is the definitive fix; tolvaptan/urea bridge
CKDImpaired free-water excretionFluid restriction less effective; urea useful; caution with loop dosing
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in SIADH: SSRIs/SNRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, thiazides, NSAIDs, antipsychotics, desmopressin, high-dose IV cyclophosphamide, MDMA — all can precipitate or worsen hyponatremia. Never give hypotonic IV fluids (D5W, ½NS) to a SIADH patient — they lower sodium further.
Monitor

Titration & follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • After fluid restriction: recheck Na in 2–3 days, then weekly until stable.
  • After urea / salt / loop: recheck within ~1 week; monitor K and renal function on the loop.
  • Tolvaptan: initiated in hospital with frequent Na; on maintenance, recheck per response and keep any rise <8 mmol/L/24h.
  • Track the underlying cause (repeat imaging, medication changes) and re-screen for occult malignancy if SIADH persists unexplained.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Relevant Grade A & B screening

There is no USPSTF recommendation to screen for SIADH itself, but its common causes are screening targets — especially lung cancer (the classic malignant driver):

GradeRecommendationPopulation
BAnnual low-dose CT lung cancer screeningAdults 50–80 with ≥20 pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within 15 years
BTobacco cessation counseling + pharmacotherapyAll adults who use tobacco
BDepression screening (with adequate systems for treatment)Adults — relevant because SSRIs used for depression are a leading drug cause
AUnhealthy alcohol use screening + brief counselingAdults ≥18 — alcohol misuse both causes hyponatremia and is a major ODS risk factor
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED / admit for: serum Na <125 with symptoms; any seizure, marked confusion, vomiting, or somnolence; a documented acute drop; suspected acute cause; or need for hypertonic saline or hospital-initiated tolvaptan.

Refer to nephrology/endocrinology for refractory chronic SIADH (failing restriction + solute), tolvaptan candidacy, or diagnostic uncertainty (SIADH vs CSW vs reset osmostat).

🛏️ Wards — acute correction, safely capped
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria

  • Symptomatic hyponatremia (moderately-severe or severe symptoms), or
  • Na <125 mmol/L (moderate–profound) even if minimally symptomatic, or
  • Acute drop, high ODS risk, or need for 3% saline / tolvaptan initiation / frequent Na monitoring, or
  • Failure of, or unsafe, outpatient management.
The admission question is not just "how low?" but "how fast, how symptomatic, and how risky to correct?" A chronic Na of 122 in a stable outpatient may be managed closely as an outpatient; an acute 128 with vomiting is admitted.

Algorithm

Correction decision map

Symptoms → chronicity → the correction ceiling → watch for and rescue overcorrection. The ceiling is a limit, not a target.
Treat

Acute management ladder

💊

By symptom severity — with doses & the safety ceiling

1
Severe symptoms → 3% hypertonic saline NOW
Seizures, coma, vomiting, respiratory distress — regardless of chronicity
▾
3% saline (513 mmol/L Na) directly adds sodium faster than the kidney excretes it — the only rapid reversal of life-threatening cerebral edema. A 4–6 mmol/L rise is usually enough to abort herniation/seizure; you do not normalize Na acutely.
ProtocolBolusRepeatEarly target
2013 US Expert Panel100 mL 3% NaCl IV over 10 minUp to 2 more times (max 3 × 100 mL) until symptoms improve~4–6 mmol/L rise in first hours
2014 European guideline150 mL 3% NaCl IV over 20 minRecheck Na, repeat 150 mL over 20 min until 5 mmol/L rise (≤~2 further boluses)5 mmol/L rise in the first hour
Boluses are now preferred over continuous infusions for symptomatic patients — safer and easier to control. Do not chase a "normal" number; chase symptom resolution and the 4–6 mmol/L early bump.
2
Moderately-severe symptoms
Nausea, confusion, headache without vomiting
▾

Single 150 mL 3% NaCl over 20 min (European) or a controlled low-rate infusion aiming for the same modest early rise; then transition to cause-directed therapy and fluid restriction.

3
Mild / asymptomatic chronic
Cause-directed, no hypertonic saline
▾

Treat the cause, fluid restrict <1000 mL/day, add solute (urea/salt) ± loop as in the Clinic ladder. Do not give hypertonic saline for asymptomatic chronic hyponatremia — the risk is overcorrection/ODS.

!
Correction-rate ceiling — memorize
The single most important safety number
▾
WindowGeneral limitHigh-ODS-risk limit
First 24 h≤10 mmol/L (European); 10–12 (US Panel)≤8 mmol/L (aim 4–6)
First 48 h≤18 mmol/L (US Panel)≤14–16 mmol/L
Each subsequent 24 h≤8 mmol/L until Na ~130≤8 mmol/L
High-risk = Na ≤105, hypokalemia, alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease. In these patients the ceiling is ≤8 mmol/L/24h and you should plan a proactive DDAVP clamp. The limit is a ceiling, not a target.
4
DDAVP clamp — prevent overcorrection
Proactive desmopressin + controlled 3% saline
▾
once the SIADH stimulus resolves, endogenous AVP falls and the kidney abruptly dumps free water → the Na overshoots. Giving desmopressin 1–2 µg IV/SC q6–8h "clamps" AVP so water diuresis can't happen, and you raise Na predictably with titrated 3% saline to hit the daily budget (e.g., 6 mmol/L/day).

Preferred in high-ODS-risk patients (very low Na, chronic, hypokalemic). Continue until Na is safely ≥125–130 and the driver is controlled. (Sterns, CJASN 2008; proactive-vs-reactive RCT, Sci Rep 2024.)

↺
Overcorrected? Re-lower
Rescue prevents ODS
▾
  • Stop all active correction, salt, and aquaresis.
  • D5W (5% dextrose) 10 mL/kg over 1 h (free-water replacement, 2014 European guideline), AND/OR
  • Desmopressin 2 µg IV q8h to halt free-water diuresis.
  • Recheck Na q1–2h; goal is to pull the 24-h rise back under the ceiling. Early rescue reliably prevents ODS.
Calculate

Adrogué–Madias — ΔNa per litre

ΔNa from 1 L infusate = (Infusate Na + Infusate K − Serum Na) ÷ (TBW + 1). A planning aid — it underestimates the rise in SIADH, so it never replaces q2–6h measured Na.

—
Predicted ΔNa per litre; a 100 mL bolus ≈ 1/10 of this.

Assumes K-free infusate. The formula assumes a closed system and systematically underestimates the rise in SIADH because the kidney excretes the infused salt/water — measure Na frequently.

Monitor

What to trend daily

📈

Daily targets

  • Serum Na q4–6h during active correction (q2h on 3% saline / DDAVP clamp); loosen once stable and within limits.
  • Strict I/O, daily weight, K — remember correcting hypokalemia itself raises Na; count it toward the daily budget.
  • Urine output: a sudden large dilute urine heralds impending overcorrection → pre-empt with desmopressin.
  • Reassess symptoms and volume status; confirm the cause is being addressed.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for: active seizures, coma or airway compromise; need for repeated 3% saline boluses; Na <115–120 with severe symptoms; or need for q1–2h Na monitoring with a DDAVP clamp.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: Na ≥125–130 and rising safely within limits, symptoms resolved, cause identified/addressed, stable on an outpatient regimen (restriction ± urea/salt/tolvaptan), and reliable follow-up Na within 1 week. Educate on fluid restriction and offending-drug avoidance.

Home

Na stable, symptoms resolved, understands fluid restriction, reliable follow-up.

Home health

Needs nursing for labs/med reconciliation or teaching on restriction/urea at home.

SNF

Frail/elderly needing 24h nursing, ongoing Na monitoring, deconditioned after falls.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-fall/fracture or post-stroke functional deficits, can tolerate ≥3h therapy/day.

LTAC

Prolonged complex needs (e.g., malignancy with recurrent SIADH, vent).

Hospice / palliative

Advanced malignancy with paraneoplastic SIADH and goals of comfort.
🫀 ICU — severe symptomatic hyponatremia & ODS prevention
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When SIADH belongs in the unit

  • Seizures, coma, or respiratory arrest from hyponatremia.
  • Severe symptomatic hyponatremia needing serial 3% saline and q1–2h Na checks.
  • High-ODS-risk profile requiring a controlled DDAVP clamp.
A seizing hyponatremic patient needs 3% saline immediately — 100–150 mL bolus — alongside airway management. Do not wait for a formal workup; a 4–6 mmol/L rise is the goal to break the seizure.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Reliable IV access. 3% saline is hyperosmolar (~1027 mOsm/L); central line preferred for prolonged infusion, but short peripheral boluses of 100–150 mL are generally acceptable.
  • Serum Na q1–2h during active correction, then space out as it stabilizes within limits.
  • Foley for accurate urine output — early warning of aquaresis/overcorrection.
  • Continuous neuro monitoring; EEG if seizing or unexplained obtundation.
Protocols

Hypertonic saline & DDAVP protocols

💉

The agents that raise (or safely re-lower) sodium

AgentMechanismDoseEffectWhen to pick
3% NaCl (bolus)Adds Na (513 mmol/L) faster than renal excretion100 mL/10 min ×≤3 (US) or 150 mL/20 min repeat to 5 mmol/L rise (EU)Rapid ↑Na, reverses edemaSevere symptoms (seizure/coma)
3% NaCl (infusion)Same, continuous~0.5–2 mL/kg/h, hourly Na, formula-guidedSlow controlled ↑NaOngoing correction after boluses (boluses preferred)
Desmopressin (DDAVP clamp)V2 agonist — "clamps" AVP to block water diuresis1–2 µg IV/SC q6–8h (≈0.03 µg/kg)Predictable, slow Na rise; no overshootHigh-ODS-risk; proactive with 3% saline
D5W (5% dextrose)Free-water replacement to re-lower Na10 mL/kg over 1 h↓Na back under ceilingOvercorrection rescue
the ICU levers are opposites for a reason: 3% saline raises Na for the crisis; DDAVP + D5W stop and reverse the rise to protect against demyelination. The whole art is landing Na inside the ceiling.
Sodium chloride — the active ingredient of 3% hypertonic saline (513 mmol/L Na), the only agent that rapidly raises serum sodium in a hyponatremic emergency.

Airway

Airway & seizure control

🌬️

Support the brain while sodium recovers

Ventilation in SIADH is supportive, not therapeutic — you intubate for airway protection in coma/status or for non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, while 3% saline treats the actual problem. Hyponatremic seizures are treated by raising sodium (3% saline), not primarily by antiepileptics, though benzodiazepines bridge acutely.

Rescue

Overcorrection rescue & ODS prevention

⚙️

The central ICU concern

In chronic hyponatremia the entire ICU game is a slow, controlled, capped rise: know the limit, measure Na frequently, replace K carefully (it counts toward the Na budget), and use the DDAVP clamp / D5W rescue to stay under the ceiling. Aggressive normalization is never the goal.

SituationAction
Rise trending past 24-h ceilingStop correction → D5W 10 mL/kg over 1 h ± desmopressin 2 µg IV q8h; recheck Na q1–2h
Sudden large dilute urine outputPre-empt overshoot with desmopressin before Na jumps
High-risk from the start (Na ≤105, EtOH, malnutrition)Proactive DDAVP clamp; target only 4–6 mmol/L/day
Early re-lowering reliably prevents ODS. Once demyelination is clinically established there is no reliable treatment — so the win is entirely in prevention.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: symptoms resolved, off 3% saline, Na rising within limits, q4–6h monitoring is sufficient, and the airway is secure. Not yet if: still requiring q1–2h Na, active DDAVP clamp with unstable rise, or unresolved seizures/airway risk.

Sources, trials & credits

Landmark trials & evidence

TrialYearResultWhy it matters
SALT-1 & SALT-2 (Schrier, NEJM)2006Oral tolvaptan (15→60 mg) raised serum Na vs placebo — day 4 ΔNa 3.6–4.3 vs ~0.3; normonatremia at day 4 40–55% vs 11–13%; Na drifted back after stoppingEstablished V2 antagonism ("aquaresis") as an effective, FDA-approved SIADH therapy — and that it treats, not cures
SALTWATER (Berl, JASN)2010Open-label extension, 111 pts, mean ~701 days: sustained higher Na, acceptable safety, no drug-attributable ODSShowed long-term tolvaptan durability and safety in chronic hyponatremia
SALT post-hoc (cancer/SIADH, Cancer Med)2017Tolvaptan effective for malignancy-related SIADH hyponatremiaSupports use in the paraneoplastic (small-cell) setting
Urea cohorts (e.g., Soupart)2012Oral urea 15–30 g/day raised Na comparably to vaptans; cheap; no ODS signalBasis for the 2014 European guideline endorsing urea as second-line
Proactive vs reactive desmopressin RCT (Sci Rep)2024Proactive DDAVP clamp gave more predictable correction with less overshootSupports the proactive DDAVP-clamp strategy in high-risk patients
